items.title: [Fast Company] Former ARPA-H director Renee Wegrzyn wants to solve science’s ‘magic hands’ problem
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Renee Wegrzyn spent her career building the future of American science—including the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, or ARPA-H, the White House agency created to accelerate health breakthroughs.

Then the Trump administration showed her the door. Wegrzyn cofounded Transfyr to tackle what she calls one of the most overlooked issues in science: the magic hands problem. She explains why fixing this unglamorous bottleneck is the prerequisite for everything AI promises to deliver in medicine, and why she can feel the next Sputnik moment coming—even if she can’t quite name it yet.

This is an abridged transcript of an interview from Rapid Response, hosted by Robert Safian, former editor-in-chief of Fast Company. From the team behind the Masters of Scale podcast, Rapid Response features candid conversations with today’s top business leaders navigating real-time challenges. Subscribe to Rapid Response wherever you get your podcasts to ensure you never miss an episode.

You were at ARPA-H, the inaugural director of a White House effort to accelerate health research. You were amped up about the possibilities, but with the Trump administration, you had to pivot. Was it hard not to take it personally that they wanted different leadership?

I’ll tell you, I’m still amped up about it. It’s still an amazing idea. Obviously, DARPA [the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency] has been around for almost 80 years. I hope ARPA-H will have the same longevity and continue to live on today.

I’m a builder. I love to take things forward and really show what’s possible. So was it hard when I left? Of course it was hard. I had a really unusual appointment: I was a presidential appointee, but I was term-limited, so I served through the transition and had a few weeks in the new administration. I served in “Trump one,” by the way, as well.

So it was a great opportunity to make sure they really understood why we built the agency. We needed an ARPA-H because there was something missing in the way we were doing science broadly, which was: How do you move really quickly? How do you get focused on a problem versus building a general knowledge set? I was able to show them what we were building and convince them that it was worth keeping around. I couldn’t be more proud of the agency and its perseverance.

So your new business, Transfyr—The New York Times wrote about you, and the article kept referring to “magic hands.” I’m curious what magic hands are. What problem is Transfyr trying to solve or address?

You probably have your favorite dish, or your parents’ or grandparents’ favorite dish. Sometimes they just have the magic hands. Nobody can cook it like they do. Nobody can make it taste the special way they can. And that happens in science as well. There are some scientists who just have the knack and can deliver really great science over and over.

The challenge is that a lot of those scientists are such experts they can hardly describe what they’re doing. It’s an art in some ways. And so the magic hands idea was really a testament to what those scientists can do in the lab.

The pipeline we’re creating at Transfyr is: Can we create computer vision and perception tools to capture the work of science as it’s being done so that we understand, if the protocol says, “Mix the cells,” whether someone is inverting the tube in a certain gentle way, while another researcher may be rigorously shaking or vortexing it, which could destroy the sample?

Those little things, compounded over the many decisions a scientist may make over the course of several hours of experimentation, lead to what is called magic hands.

Was this an issue you saw at ARPA-H, the sort of breakthroughs that were trapped in a single lab in some ways?

Where that manifested at DARPA and at ARPA-H was in a realization, through my career, of how fragile breakthroughs are. Usually, the way a breakthrough is first communicated to the world is through a research publication, a Science or Nature paper. That paper is not a product. It’s not commercializable. It’s not ready for a patient that day. That’s the starting gun for what is going to happen.

The ARPAs of this world are really fantastic at getting to that initial breakthrough and demonstrating what is possible, but following through and delivering is not a 100% guaranteed activity.

When I started ARPA-H, we wanted customers, who would be the final users of that technology, to give us feedback on what we were developing so that when we got to the last day of the experiment, they were demanding that product, versus having that be the first contact with a customer, which unfortunately is pretty common around traditional grant-making organizations.

It’s rethinking how you make sure you can transfer that knowledge off the back end of a program.

Because the folks at the lab aren’t necessarily worrying about, or prioritizing, how to make it scalable. They’re just trying to see if it works. But of course, eventually we want it to be scalable.

Sometimes the folks in the lab don’t even have the expertise or understanding of who they need to talk to next to do that, right? We think about science and those transfers as handoffs. We deploy our technology to an originating lab to understand the science and what was important about that discovery, but we can also deploy it in a receiving lab so that we can see how they’re reproducing it.

And instead of the way we transfer science today, which is looking over each other’s shoulders and saying, “Oh, you’re doing it a little wrong,” we have this video-connectedness that lets us help accelerate those iterations of transferring the science.

Do you ever get frustrated about how resources are allocated in our world? You’ve put your life toward this work, and yet so much money is devoted to, I don’t know, space exploration or the next hot social app, the Meta Muse craze. How do you deal with government and how it prioritizes things?

Yeah, it’s maddening. One of the things that has me nervous right now is that I look back on the last 80 years following the Second World War. We’ve led the globe in science and engineering and innovation. Nobody who’s practicing science today has practiced science in the United States at a time when we weren’t, quote-unquote, winning from a competitiveness perspective, when we weren’t at the top.

I genuinely believe we may lose that competitiveness, that edge, that incumbency, and I’m not sure I see us fighting for it in the way that we should be. We have to deliver on what we’ve promised to do, and that’s a commitment not just to my country, but to my kids and my family. 

What I think a lot about is Sputnik moments. We’re going to look back at this moment in time like there’s something happening, and it’s going to impact whatever’s happening 20 to 50 years from now. You can feel it in the moment.

Where that happened before, of course, was Sputnik. The United States didn’t know the Soviet Union was developing that capability, and we didn’t have a counter-capability. What I realized is that each individual person has a Sputnik moment in their life that is usually health-related. My Sputnik moment was when my mother was diagnosed with cancer. That stopped everything.

Everybody has a story, whether it happened to them or their family, or if you talk to a member of Congress, something’s happening in their state that they can’t deal with.

So I’m like, “What is the Sputnik moment now?” If ARPA-H was bringing people from an unhealthy state to a healthy state, what’s happening now is taking us beyond that. If we can figure out and solve health and wellness, a lot of people talk about abundance. What is the next trajectory? What is the Sputnik that we’re working toward?

items.title: [sootoday.com] Canada plans to bar MAID for mental illness alone indefinitely, decriminalize advance requests
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Canada will indefinitely exclude people whose sole underlying condition is mental illness from medical assistance in dying (MAID), Justice Minister Sean Fraser said Oct. 7, announcing plans for legislation this fall [cbc.ca#1][nationalpost.com#1][sootoday.com#1]. The government also plans to decriminalize advance requests for people with incurable, progressive illnesses who consent while capable but later lose that capacity. Provinces would decide whether to permit the practice through their health systems [cbc.ca#1][nationalpost.com#1][hs.fi#1]. Fraser cited concerns about inadequate access to mental-health care and the lack of medical agreement on when some mental illnesses can be considered irremediable [cbc.ca#1][sootoday.com#1]. A joint House-Senate committee recommended an indefinite exclusion in June, while some members issued dissenting opinions criticizing the committee’s process [nationalpost.com#1][graphic.com.gh#1]. The exclusion is due to expire March 17, 2027, so the legislation must pass both chambers before then to prevent the scheduled expansion [sootoday.com#1][catholicregister.org#1]. On Oct. 7, MPs defeated Conservative MP Tamara Jansen’s bill on the same subject, 187-141; a legal challenge to the existing exclusion remains before the courts [cbc.ca#1][sootoday.com#1][graphic.com.gh#1].

items.title: [WIRED] Humans Watched This Supernova Explode Nearly a Millennium Ago. Now You Can See It in High Definition
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Astronomers have obtained the most detailed image to date of the Pa 30 nebula, the remnants of a supernova famous for having likely been observed and documented from Earth during the Middle Ages. Now, the new photograph reveals structures that had long gone unnoticed. Previous images of the explosion’s remnants had also captured a sphere of long, filament-like strands of matter that collectively resemble fireworks or a dandelion. The new observations, made with the Gemini North telescope in Hawaii, revealed about 10 times more structures than any previous glimpses of the supernova remnant.

Previously believed to be harmless, P3 can form harmful-looking protein clumps even faster than amyloid beta and may also damage brain cells.

items.title: [Macworld] M6 deep dive: Brilliant 2nm design, but short on bandwidth
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Macworld

Our own review of the new Mac mini analyzed the performance and value of the M5 Pro version, but that chip has been around since the spring. Far more interesting is the M6, a new-generation processor made on TSMC’s 2nm process and sporting some interesting architectural changes. Our German sister site Macwelt reviewed that model, and found it to be a big jump over the preview Mac mini, which came equipped with an M4.

Now that the chip has been out for a couple of weeks, we’re starting to get some good technical breakdowns that discuss the finer architectural details of the chip. (Two of our favorites are Geekerwan and High Yield / SemiAnalysis.) They paint the picture of a processor with an interesting set of new advancements, primarily the result of TSMC’s new 2nm process and the increased density it enables. Here are some of the things we learned.

What 2nm enables

Along with the A20 Pro in the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo, the M6 represents the first of Apple’s chips to use the new 2nm manufacturing process from TSMC, and it’s one of the first mass-market 2nm chips in the world.

New manufacturing process technologies can be tricky to understand, but in essence, this new 2nm process has smaller features—gates and transistors and resistors and such—which means the same logic and RAM storage can fit into a smaller area. You can use this to make a smaller chip, or just to fit more chip “stuff” in the same area.

In the case of the M6, it allows Apple to increase core counts and add features while actually making the chip slightly smaller than the M5. The M6 is estimated to be about 142 mm2, compared to the M5’s 157 mm2. In fact, with the exception of the 119 mm2 M1, the M6 is the smallest M-series chip yet.

SemiAnalysis

This new manufacturing process brings more than just smaller, denser chip features. It also gives us a new type of transistor, GAAFET (gate-all-around field-effect transistor), which replaces the older FinFET design. It surrounds the gate material on all four sides, vs. just three sides as in the FinFET technology. It reduces leakage and makes the chips more electrically stable, so they can run at lower power and higher clock speeds.

Big CPU changes

With the M5, Apple rebranded its performance cores as “super cores.” In the M5 Pro and Max, the company used both the new super cores and new mid-range performance cores. Some chips, such as the A18 Pro, included both super and efficiency cores.

The M6 is the first Apple processor to use three different CPU core designs: 2 Super cores, 4 Performance cores, and 6 Efficiency cores. It’s not the first company to do this sort of thing, as Intel’s Panther Lake generation includes a 4-8-4 design with what it calls performance cores, efficiency cores, and low-power efficiency cores.

This new middle-child performance core is about half the size of a super core, and while not as fast, it’s a lot more powerful than the efficiency cores. So in essence, Apple took the four super and six efficiency CPU-core setup of the M5, and traded out two of the super cores for four Performance cores. It’s a good design, as it improves multi-core CPU performance greatly while not having a big impact on CPU die area or single-thread performance.

Foundry

The cache setup is similar to the M5 in many ways. The SLC (system-level cache, shared by all of the SoC’s components) is still 16 megabytes. The L2 cache has gone up to 20MB from 16MB in the M5, and it’s shared by the super cores and performance cores. Since it is now being used by six CPU cores instead of four, an equal increase in size makes sense. As with the M5, the super cores are weird in that they also have their own individual 1.5MB L2 caches in addition to the big shared L2.

The efficiency cores are said to be identical to those in the A20 Pro, and they’re quite capable in their own right, but they have their own separate L2 cache and AMX unit (a CPU complex dedicated to speeding up matrix math operations).

This is one of the biggest fundamental changes in the M6—a new three-tier CPU core setup, with S-cores that are more powerful and clocked higher than those in earlier processors. We’ll probably see this three-tier setup in the M7 as well.

A GPU starved for bandwidth?

Apple added two more GPU cores in the M6 compared to the M5, taking it from 10 cores to 12. This alone accounts for a 20 percent increase in peak GPU compute performance, but it’s also clocked slightly higher. The new core design does have faster geometry processing rates (important for 3D graphics scenes with complex geometry), but it’s mostly this core count and clock speed boost that is responsible for the better performance.

In real-world applications, we can’t help but think the GPU is limited by memory bandwidth. The M6 has a max memory bandwidth of 170 GB/sec, but only in the 24GB and 32GB models, which have LPDDR 5x RAM at 10,667 MT/sec. The 16GB model has slower memory running at 9,600 MT/sec, giving it the same 153 GB/sec as the M5.

That’s not a very big increase in memory bandwidth, especially when you consider it’s being shared with the CPU cores and Neural Engine.

Foundry

Despite a very modest increase in memory bandwidth, the increase in GPU cores and clock speeds helps the M6 improve 3D graphics performance by 20 percent or more. We’re left wondering: How much faster would it be with more memory bandwidth available?

If you’re going to add CPU cores, double Neural Engine cores, and add 25% more GPU cores while only increasing memory bandwidth by 10%, you would expect to be limited by memory bandwidth at almost every turn. The M6 has plenty of cache, but the A20 Pro just goes to show how much performance you can get from a wider memory bus, and it’s time for Apple to do the same for the base M-series chips as well.

Double Neural Engine

Speaking of memory-hungry operations, the M6 has the same doubled-up Neural Engine as the A20 Pro. It’s technically two separate 16-core Neural Engine units rather than a single 32-core one. Each 16-core cluster has its own separate cache that isn’t shared with the other, but there’s a single control unit for the entire array.

Foundry

It’s hard to know if this 16/16 split affects real-world performance more than just having a big 32-core Neural Engine with a single cache that’s twice as big, but we do see some nice performance gains, with the M6 running quantized models on the Neural Engine about 50 percent faster than the M4, and even 20 percent faster than the M5 Pro despite having a lot less memory bandwidth.

Still, it’s important to recognize that twice the cores does not equal twice the performance, especially if the system is limited in some other way. Again, we have to wonder if memory bandwidth is holding things back here.

M7 has one job: a wider memory bus

If the most recent rumors are to be believed, the M6 will be the only chip in this generation. We would typically either have an M6 Pro already, or get it in the spring of 2027, along with an M6 Max and even potentially an M6 Ultra. Then, Apple would start the next generation with the M7 in the fall of 2027.

Instead, so the rumors go, the M7 is being pulled in and will ship in the spring, with the M7 Pro/Max variants in the fall. This would leave the M6 as the sole chip in this generation.

Apple is said to be doing this primarily to accelerate the roadmap of its chips’ AI performance, and it’s easy to see why. The M6 has a 128-bit memory interface, the same as every base M-series chip since the M1. The only thing improving memory bandwidth is faster DRAM chips.

AI tasks, whether they are performed by the Neural Engine or the GPU, tend to be very memory intensive. We’ve seen how much the A20 Pro’s performance benefitted from increasing the memory bus by 50 percent from 64-bit to 96-bit, and it’s definitely time for the M series to do the same.

Yes, we expect architectural advancements in the CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine cores of the M7, but no single change would be as significant as increasing the memory bus to 192-bit or 256-bit. This would increase memory bandwidth to 255 GB/sec or 341 GB/sec with the same LPDDR5x memory and make graphics, GPU compute, and intensive AI tasks just fly.
